Q: Missing selection for device in app inspector A:

En Android Studio, la opción para seleccionar el dispositivo en el Inspector (Database Inspector o Layout Inspector) aparece en la ventana de “Running Devices” cuando tu app está ejecutándose en un emulador o dispositivo físico conectado. Si no ves la lista, es porque no hay procesos depurables activos, ejecuta en un emulador o dispositivo físico conectado por USB con depuración habilitada,

Abre la ventana de Running Devices (parte inferior derecha de Android Studio).

  1. Haz clic en Toggle Layout Inspector o en el botón del Database Inspector.

  2. El inspector se conectará automáticamente al proceso depurable en primer plano del dispositivo seleccionado,

    No hay app en ejecución: El inspector solo muestra dispositivos cuando hay un proceso depurable activo.

    1. Depuración USB deshabilitada: En tu dispositivo físico, activa Opciones de desarrollador → Depuración USB.

    2. ADB no reconoce el dispositivo: Ejecuta adb devices en la terminal para confirmar que tu dispositivo está conectado.

    3. Versión de Android Studio: En versiones recientes, el inspector se integra directamente con la ventana de dispositivos; ya no aparece como menú separado.

    4. Configuración de atributos de vista: Para el Layout Inspector, asegúrate de que la opción debug_view_attributes esté habilitada automáticamente por Android Studio (se puede forzar con adb shell settings put global debug_view_attributes 1,

      1. Si usas Database Inspector, primero ejecuta la app en modo depuración; luego el inspector mostrará la lista de bases de datos disponibles en el dispositivo seleccionado.

      2. Si usas Layout Inspector, asegúrate de que la actividad esté en primer plano; el inspector se engancha solo a procesos visibles.

      3. Si cambias entre varios dispositivos, el inspector se conecta automáticamente al que esté activo, pero puedes elegir manualmente en la ventana de Running Devices.

Q: Why does zsh generate zcompdump files in ZDOTDIR even when a different location is specified when calling compinit? A:

The two most common reasons this happens:

1. You are using a Zsh framework (like Oh My Zsh or Zim)

Frameworks handle completion initialization automatically and will bundle their own implicit calls to compinit.

* The Culprit: If you place compinit -d ... before sourcing the framework, the framework's internal scripts will run compinit again later, generating the fallback dump file in your $ZDOTDIR.

* The Fix: Most frameworks provide a specific environment variable to set the dump path directly. For Oh My Zsh, define ZSH_COMPDUMP before sourcing oh-my-zsh.sh:

export ZSH_COMPDUMP="$XDG_CACHE_HOME/zsh/zcompdump"

source $ZSH/oh-my-zsh.sh

2. Your OS runs a global compinit

Certain Linux distributions (like Ubuntu and Debian) trigger compinit out of the box in system-wide configuration files before your user profile ever loads.

* The Culprit: /etc/zsh/zshrc triggers a default compinit call, which creates the file in your $ZDOTDIR or $HOME before your personal .zshrc ever gets executed.

* The Fix: Tell Zsh to skip the system-wide completion setup by adding this flag to your .zshenv file (which runs before the global zshrc):

skip_global_compinit=1

How to diagnose

To pinpoint exactly which script is sneaking in the extra call, run a trace on a new shell session and filter for compinit:

zsh -ixc : 2>&1 | grep compinit

This outputs every line where compinit gets evaluated, along with the exact file path responsible

for triggering it.

Q: Constructor process that might fail. Proper way to handle this. A try catch where is the class instance? private constructor + public static member? A:

for now, the way to work this has been the next:

  • A private constructor.
  • Calling the private constructor from a public static member function, with the purpose of being able to return a value (if needed) that could indicate some error code.

This is not an option unless you are talking about a singleton. If you are talking about a singleton, there's no need to make the singleton member a static since there will only be one instance of said member anyway. This option should not be considered.

  • At the place where is the class instance, a free function, putting a try catch, to in that way, if there is some fail in the constructor, then the idea is to provide to the user a set of possible actions to continue, i.e. at this specific point the idea is not simply to terminate the program. The reason about placing a try catch in the caller side is for a centralized handling, taking into account there are several classes with member functions with the same interface and functionality equivalence.

This is feasible and has precedence. The standard library has a mix for classes and functions.

  • Some classes throw an exception upon instantiation. These can't be instantiated having an invalid state. For example, std::regex and std::thread.
  • Some are constructed but keep a state that can be checked after construction. This is the default for the std::fstream type of classes. You can may fstreams throwing, but it usually turns a one-liner into; construct, change the throwing-state, then open the file. It's cumbersome and rarely used.
  • Some let you as a user choose what behavior you want. Functions of this type may have a non-throwing overload that takes a std::error_code& instead of throwing. Classes in the std::filesystem sub-library offer the same choice.

Any of these three patterns would work for your scenario so pick whichever fits how you want failure to surface to the caller.

Aside: What you most probably should not do is to add exception handling around your class' or function's inner workings unless it is using classes or functions that may throw and the user has called a non-throwing API. Otherwise, document what may be thrown and let the exception out.

Q: Strange "pattern not match" error on fluentd A:

The problem is that these ELB-HealthChecker line log has an empty referer ip field. And then the log doesn't match apache2 log format for fluentd.

So the way to fix that is to filter logs with ELB-HealthChecker user-agent.

Q: Find value in a multi-dimensional array A:

Try this

For n = 1 To UBound(myArray, 1)
    If myArray(n, 1) = myString Then
        myTimeStamp = myArray(n, 2) 'find the timestamp of this string in col2
        myTimeDiff = DateDiff("n", myTimeStamp, DateTime.Now()) ' calculate the time difference in minutes
        myIndex = n 'return the array index (n)
    End If
Next n
